messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Thomas, a 77-year-old North American male and retired delivery driver, first presented with symptoms after a traumatic assault several months ago. He was working late one evening, delivering packages in an unfamiliar part of town, when he encountered a group of individuals who attacked him. Mr. Thomas found himself overwhelmed by the sudden violence, unable to defend himself adequately. The assault left him not only physically injured but also deeply shaken mentally. In the weeks following the incident, Mr. Thomas began to experience profound self-doubt and questioned his ability to handle everyday tasks. He had come to believe that he could no longer trust his judgment or act appropriately in dangerous situations. This sense of doubt was compounded by shattered beliefs about the world’s safety, leaving him feeling vulnerable and uncertain at every turn. To cope with these overwhelming feelings, Mr. Thomas adopted several maladaptive strategies. He found himself eating excessively, often reaching for high-calorie foods that provided temporary relief from his anxiety. Overeating became a means to manage the distress he felt whenever thoughts of the assault surfaced. This behavior was further reinforced by his tendency to keep busy, working tirelessly around the house or taking on additional tasks to distract himself from the trauma. Mr. Thomas’s wife noted that he had become increasingly withdrawn and preoccupied with his work, often spending long hours in the garage or completing odd jobs around their home. These behaviors were not just a sign of busyness but also an active attempt to avoid thinking about the assault. He believed that if he thought too much about what happened, he would be unable to handle it. The self-doubt and shattered beliefs continued to influence his behavior. Mr. Thomas had started eating more and more as a way to numb his emotional pain, leading to noticeable weight gain. His preoccupation with keeping busy also extended into his interactions with others. He avoided social gatherings or any situations that might trigger memories of the assault. What frightened him most was the fear of not being able to protect himself again. This constant threat monitoring made it difficult for him to engage in activities he once enjoyed, such as going on walks or attending community events. His wife expressed concern about his increasing isolation and how these behaviors were affecting their relationship. Mr. Thomas finally sought help when his wife insisted that he see a therapist, noting the significant changes in his behavior and mood. He was most afraid of losing control again but hoped that with support, he could regain some sense of normalcy and trust in himself and the world around him. The tightening loop of negative appraisals leading to maladaptive strategies had become increasingly burdensome, affecting not only his daily life but also his marriage. Through this journey, Mr. Thomas’s self-doubt and shattered beliefs continued to reinforce his maladaptive coping mechanisms, making it challenging for him to break the cycle without professional intervention. His current state was one of profound distress, with a deep-seated need for support and understanding as he navigated the aftermath of the assault.
